key_insight: Machine-learned long-time simulations reveal that small polarons at oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move orders of magnitude more slowly than in bulk because surface pathways are severely constrained.
engineering_relevance: The results explain why porous rutile TiO2 can show much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for designing better oxides for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended a machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics framework to a redox-active oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale dynamics across multiple temperatures on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Mapped polaron hopping pathways and vacancy-induced free-energy shifts at the surface.
evidence_signal: Several nanoseconds of temperature-dependent dynamics showed orders-of-magnitude suppressed surface polaron mobility, with motion mostly limited to planar inter-row hops and rare interlayer transitions.
watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on a single prototypical oxide surface, so transferability and accuracy on other reduced oxides or defect chemistries still need validation.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
